p.src: Now Jiang Wei, fearing that reinforcements would arrive, first withdrew the infantry with all the weapons, carts, baggage, and other military supplies, then left the cavalry to cover the rear. A scout reported this to Deng Ai. Deng Ai laughed and said, “Jiang Wei knows that the Grand General is coming, and so he has withdrawn first. There is no need to pursue him; if we do, we shall fall into his trap.” He therefore sent men to reconnoitre, and they returned to report that bundles of firewood and dry grass had indeed been heaped in the narrow reaches of Luo Valley, ready to burn the pursuing troops. All acclaimed Deng Ai, saying, “General, your foresight is truly divine!” He then dispatched an envoy bearing a memorial to report the matter to the throne. Sima Zhao was greatly delighted and again petitioned that Deng Ai be rewarded.

p.src: Meanwhile, when Sun Chen, Grand General of Eastern Wu, learned that Quan Duan, Tang Zi, and the others had surrendered to Wei, he flew into a rage and had every member of their families put to death. The ruler of Wu, Sun Liang, was then only seventeen. Seeing that Sun Chen’s slaughter had gone too far, he deeply disapproved. One day, while visiting the Western Garden, he ate some unripe plums and ordered a palace attendant to fetch honey. It was soon brought, but when he saw several pieces of mouse droppings in it, he summoned the keeper of the stores and rebuked him. The keeper knocked his head upon the ground and said, “I keep it tightly sealed. How could mouse droppings have entered?” Sun Liang asked, “Has this attendant ever asked you for honey to eat?” The keeper replied, “Several days ago he did ask me for honey, but I truly dared not give him any.” Pointing at the attendant, Sun Liang said, “You must have been angry that the keeper refused you honey, so you put the droppings into it to frame him.” The attendant denied the charge. Sun Liang said, “This is easily determined. If the droppings had long been in the honey, they would be wet both inside and out; if they were newly placed there, they would be wet outside but dry within.” He ordered them cut open and examined; sure enough, they were dry inside. The attendant confessed his guilt. Such, in general, was Sun Liang’s intelligence. Yet for all his intelligence, Sun Chen held him in his grasp, and he could exercise no authority of his own. Sun Chen’s younger brother Sun Ju, General Who Inspires Awe Afar, entered the Canglong Gate to command the palace guard; Sun En, General of the Martial Guard, Sun Gan, General of the Household, and Sun Kai, Commandant of Changshui, separately garrisoned the various camps.

p.src: One day, as the ruler of Wu, Sun Liang, sat despondently, the Palace Gentleman of the Yellow Gate Quan Ji was at his side. Quan Ji was the emperor’s brother-in-law. Sun Liang tearfully confided to him, “Sun Chen monopolizes power and kills at whim; his contempt for Us is intolerable. If we do not act against him now, he will surely become a future scourge.” Quan Ji said, “If Your Majesty has any use for me, I will not shrink even from ten thousand deaths.” Sun Liang said, “You must muster the imperial guards at once and, together with General Liu Cheng, secure the city gates. We shall go out in person and kill Sun Chen. But you must on no account let your mother learn of this. Your mother is Sun Chen’s elder sister. Should the secret leak, the harm to Us would be no small matter.” Quan Ji said, “I beg Your Majesty to draft an edict for me. When the deed is undertaken, I shall show the edict to the assembled men, so that none of Sun Chen’s followers will dare make a reckless move.” Sun Liang agreed and immediately wrote a secret edict and entrusted it to Quan Ji. Quan Ji received the edict and returned home, where he secretly told his father, Quan Shang. On learning of the affair, Quan Shang told his wife, “Within three days Sun Chen will be killed.” His wife said, “It is right to kill him.” Though she assented in words, she secretly sent a letter to inform Sun Chen. Sun Chen flew into a rage. That very night he summoned his four brothers, mustered his finest troops, and first surrounded the imperial palace; at the same time, he arrested Quan Shang, Liu Cheng, and all their households. By daybreak, the ruler of Wu, Sun Liang, heard a great din of gongs and drums outside the palace gates. A palace attendant rushed in and reported, “Sun Chen has led his troops to surround the inner gardens.” Sun Liang was furious. Pointing at Empress Quan, he cursed, “Your father and brother have ruined Our great undertaking!” He drew his sword and made to go out. Empress Quan, the attendants, and the close ministers all clung to his robes and wept, refusing to let him leave. After Sun Chen had put Quan Shang, Liu Cheng, and the others to death, he summoned the civil and military officials to court and proclaimed, “The sovereign has long been debauched and infirm, benighted, disorderly, and devoid of the Way. He is unfit to serve the ancestral temples and must now be deposed. Any civil or military official who dares disobey shall be judged guilty of treason!” All were afraid and answered, “We shall obey the General’s command.” Huan Yi, the Imperial Secretary, was enraged. He strode boldly from the ranks, pointed at Sun Chen, and reviled him: “Our present sovereign is a wise and discerning ruler. How dare you utter such rebellious words! I would sooner die than obey the command of a traitorous minister.” Sun Chen flew into a rage, drew his own sword, and struck him down. He then entered the palace, pointed at the ruler of Wu, Sun Liang, and cursed him: “You are a benighted and unprincipled sovereign who ought by rights to be put to death, as an apology to all beneath Heaven! Out of regard for the late emperor, I shall merely depose you as Prince of Kuaiji and choose a virtuous man to enthrone in your place!” He shouted at Li Chong, a Gentleman of the Palace Secretariat, to seize Sun Liang’s imperial seal and sash, and ordered Deng Cheng to take him into custody. Sun Liang departed in bitter tears. A later poet lamented in verse:

p.src: Sun Chen sent Sun Kai, Minister of the Imperial Clan, and Dong Chao, a Gentleman of the Palace Secretariat, to Hulin to welcome Sun Xiu, Prince of Langya, and invite him to become ruler. Sun Xiu, whose style was Zilie, was Sun Quan’s sixth son. While at Hulin, he dreamed one night that he rode a dragon into the heavens. Looking back, he could not see its tail, and awoke with a start. The next day Sun Kai and Dong Chao arrived, bowed before him, and invited him to return to the capital. When he reached Qu’e, an old man who called himself Gan Xiu knocked his head upon the ground and said, “Prolonged affairs inevitably change. I beg Your Highness to travel swiftly.” Sun Xiu thanked him. When he reached Busai Pavilion, General Sun En came with the imperial carriage to receive him. Sun Xiu dared not ride in the imperial carriage and entered instead in a small cart. The hundred officials bowed to him beside the road, and Sun Xiu hastily alighted and returned their salutations. Sun Chen came out, ordered attendants to help him rise, and invited him into the great hall, where he ascended the imperial seat and assumed the throne. Only after repeatedly declining the honor did Sun Xiu accept the imperial jade seal. When the civil and military officials had finished offering their congratulations, a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the realm, and the era was changed to the first year of Yong’an. Sun Chen was enfeoffed as Chancellor and Governor of Jingzhou; the many officials each received ranks and rewards; and Sun Hao, the son of Sun Xiu’s elder brother, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wucheng. Five members of Sun Lin’s clan were marquises, and all commanded the imperial guards; their power overshadowed that of the sovereign. The ruler of Wu, Sun Xiu, feared that he might stir up trouble within the court, so outwardly he showed him favor while inwardly remaining on his guard. Sun Chen grew more arrogant and overbearing than ever.

p.src: In the twelfth month of winter, Sun Chen brought an ox and wine into the palace to offer birthday felicitations. When the ruler of Wu, Sun Xiu, refused them, Sun Chen became angry and took the ox and wine to the residence of the General of the Left, Zhang Bu, where they drank together. When the wine had taken hold, he said to Zhang Bu, “When I first deposed the Prince of Kuaiji, everyone urged me to become sovereign. I believed the present ruler to be virtuous, and therefore enthroned him. Now I offer him birthday felicitations and am rebuffed: he treats me as a man of no account. Sooner or later I shall show you what I mean!” Zhang Bu heard him and merely murmured agreement. The next day Zhang Bu entered the palace and secretly reported Sun Chen’s words to Sun Xiu. Sun Xiu was greatly afraid and found no peace by day or night. Within a few days, Sun Chen sent Meng Zong, a Gentleman of the Palace Secretariat, with fifteen thousand elite soldiers drawn from the Central Camp to garrison Wuchang; he also gave him all the weapons in the imperial arsenal. Thereupon General Wei Miao and Shi Shuo of the Martial Guard secretly reported to Sun Xiu, “Sun Chen has deployed troops outside the capital and emptied the imperial arsenal of weapons. Sooner or later he will surely revolt.” Sun Xiu was greatly alarmed and urgently summoned Zhang Bu to discuss a plan. Zhang Bu advised, “The veteran general Ding Feng is a man of surpassing strategy who can decide matters of great consequence. Your Majesty should consult him.” Sun Xiu therefore summoned Ding Feng into the palace and secretly told him the whole affair. Ding Feng said, “Your Majesty need not worry. I have a plan to rid the state of this scourge.” Sun Xiu asked what the plan was. Ding Feng replied, “At tomorrow’s La Festival, simply announce a great banquet for all the ministers and summon Sun Chen to attend. I shall make all the necessary arrangements.” Sun Xiu was overjoyed. Ding Feng assigned Wei Miao and Shi Shuo to manage affairs outside, while Zhang Bu was to act as their confederate within.

p.src: That night a furious gale arose, sending sand flying and stones rolling, and tearing old trees up by the roots. At daybreak the wind subsided, and an envoy came by imperial command to invite Sun Chen to a banquet in the palace. Sun Chen had just risen from bed when, on level ground, he fell as though someone had pushed him, leaving him ill at ease. More than ten envoys crowded around and escorted him inside. His family tried to stop him, saying, “The fierce wind raged all night, and this morning you fell for no reason. We fear these are evil omens; you must not attend the banquet.” Chen said, “My brothers and I jointly command the palace guards. Who would dare come near me? If anything happens, set fire to the residence as a signal.” Having given these instructions, he mounted his carriage and entered the palace. Sun Xiu, ruler of Wu, hastily descended from the imperial seat to welcome him and invited Chen to take the place of honor. After several rounds of wine, the company cried in alarm, “A fire can be seen outside the palace!” Chen immediately made to rise. Xiu stopped him, saying, “Be at ease, Chancellor. There are ample troops outside; what need is there to fear?” Before he had finished speaking, General of the Left Zhang Bu came rushing into the hall with sword drawn and more than thirty warriors behind him, shouting sternly, “By imperial decree, seize the traitor Sun Chen!” Chen tried desperately to flee, but the warriors had already seized him. Chen knocked his head on the ground and pleaded, “I beg to be exiled to Jiaozhou and allowed to retire to the fields.” Xiu rebuked him: “Why did you not exile Teng Yin, Lü Ju, and Wang Dun?” He ordered Chen to be dragged away and beheaded. Zhang Bu thereupon dragged Sun Chen down to the east side of the hall and beheaded him. None of Chen’s followers dared move. Zhang Bu proclaimed the decree: “The guilt rests with Sun Chen alone; no others will be called to account.” Only then were the people reassured. Zhang Bu invited Sun Xiu to ascend the Five Phoenix Tower. Ding Feng, Wei Miao, Shi Shuo, and the others arrived with Sun Chen’s brothers in custody. Xiu ordered them all beheaded in the marketplace. Several hundred members of his clan and faction were put to death, and his three kindreds were exterminated. Soldiers were ordered to dig open Sun Jun’s grave and mutilate his corpse. The tombs of the murdered Zhuge Ke, Teng Yin, Lü Ju, Wang Dun, and their families were rebuilt to honor their loyalty. All those implicated and exiled to distant lands were pardoned and allowed to return home. Ding Feng received further titles and rewards.

p.src: A dispatch was sped to Chengdu with the news. Liu Shan, the Latter Ruler, sent an envoy to offer congratulations, and the Wu envoy Xue Xu returned the courtesy. When Xue Xu returned from Shu, Sun Xiu, ruler of Wu, asked what had lately been happening there. Xue Xu reported, “Recently the Palace Regular Attendant Huang Hao has held sway, and most of the high ministers fawn upon him. When I entered their court, I heard no forthright counsel; when I passed through their countryside, the people wore the pallor of hunger. It is just as the saying goes: ‘Sparrows nesting in a hall know nothing of the great house about to burn.’” Xiu sighed, “Had Marquis Zhuge still been alive, how could matters ever have come to this?” He then wrote another state letter and had it carried to Chengdu, warning that Sima Zhao would soon usurp Wei and would surely invade Wu and Shu to display his might, so both states should make their preparations.

p.src: When Jiang Wei heard this news, he was delighted and submitted another memorial proposing an expedition against Wei. It was the winter of the first year of Jingyao in Shu-Han. Grand General Jiang Wei appointed Liao Hua and Zhang Yi as vanguard, Wang Han and Jiang Bin to the left army, Jiang Shu and Fu Qian to the right army, and Hu Ji to command the rear. Jiang Wei and Xiahou Ba jointly commanded the central army. They raised two hundred thousand troops of Shu, took leave of the Latter Ruler, and proceeded straight to Hanzhong, where Jiang Wei consulted Xiahou Ba about which place they should attack first. Xiahou Ba said, “Mount Qi is a country made for war, and troops can advance through it. That is why the late Chancellor made six expeditions from Mount Qi. There is no route through any other place.” Jiang Wei accepted his counsel and ordered the whole army to advance toward Mount Qi, where they encamped at the mouth of the valley. At the time, Deng Ai was in the stronghold at Mount Qi, mustering and inspecting the troops of Longyou. Suddenly a swift courier arrived to report that the Shu army had established three camps at the mouth of the valley. On hearing this, Deng Ai climbed to high ground to look. He returned to camp, convened his officers, and exclaimed with delight, “It is just as I expected!” Deng Ai, it transpired, had already surveyed the lay of the land and had deliberately left that place for the Shu troops to encamp; beneath the ground, from the Mount Qi stronghold straight to the Shu camp, he had already dug a tunnel, intending to strike through it when the Shu army arrived. Now Jiang Wei had divided his forces into three camps at the valley mouth, and the tunnel ran directly beneath the left camp, where Wang Han and Jiang Bin were stationed. Deng Ai summoned his son Deng Zhong and Shi Zuan, ordering each to lead ten thousand troops in assaults from the left and right; he then summoned his deputy Zheng Lun and ordered him to lead five hundred sappers through the tunnel at the second watch that very night, straight into the left camp, and burst from the ground behind the command tent.

p.src: The next day, the two armies drew up before Mount Qi.
